Quick SE note — putting together the numbers Camila requested. High level guidance that I will include in the model:

Continuous-batching assumptions (for FintechCo profile)
- Workload: steady 24/7 short-requests (avg 120 tokens) is ideal for continuous batching. With steady arrival rates we expect consistent micro-batches that increase GPU utilization without large latency tails.
- Typical batching factor: for 120-token total (40 in / 80 out) and the concurrency profile Alex shared, we expect an observed batching factor of ~1.6–2.0x vs strictly single-request execution (depends on arrival jitter and allowed queueing).
- Latency delta: with a batching target that keeps added queueing under 40ms, typical p95 latency impact is ~20–60ms (depends on model and hardware). You can tune this tradeoff: tighter latency -> lower batching factor -> higher unit cost.

Sample unit economics (ballpark estimates to include in the deck) — these are conservative hosted estimates before any reserved discounts:
- Pay-as-you-go (hosted): ~$15–18 per 1M tokens (expected range) for 80M/month steady with continuous batching applied.
- Moderate commit (3–6 month, ~300M/month commit): ~$9–12 per 1M tokens (committed pricing, lowers unit cost materially).
- Factors that change the numbers: model size (Llama-2-medium vs larger), quantization/kerning, and KV cache reuse for multi-turn conversations.

Notes on concurrency & batching interaction
- Bursty concurrency (50–60 concurrent) can reduce batching efficiency if bursts are very short; we model with an expected 2.5x peak factor and still achieve a ~1.6x batching factor overall.
- Recommend a hybrid approach: small reserved pool + payg overflow to keep tail latency predictable during bursts while getting committed-unit economics for baseline traffic.

I will put together a short slide and a worked example (cost vs tokens at 80M and 300M) and send ahead of the call.

Attaching: batching-runbook.pdf (SE notes & expected compute profiles).
